text: You wake up at seven in the morning
and pour yourself a glass of water.
Your roommate walks into the kitchen,
rubs his eyes,
and smiles.
Morning.
Did you sleep well,
he asks.
Yeah, slept like a rock,
you reply.
And right above your lips,
a bright crimson box flashes:
Lie.
Rated eighty-four percent.
You freeze.
Your roommate looks at the
breakfast you made and says,
thanks, this tastes amazing.
Floating right above his mouth in bold red letters:
Lie.
He thinks it is cold and bland.
For the next seven days,
every spoken word in your world comes
with a verified truth rating.
Green for absolute truth.
Bright crimson for deception.
You think this power will give
you the ultimate advantage.
You think you will finally know who to trust.
Instead, by day seven,
you will understand the terrifying truth:
Honesty does not save relationships.
Kindness does.
And polite lies are the only reason
society has not burned to the ground.
By noon on day one,
you are sitting in a team meeting at work.
Your manager clicks to the next slide and says,
I really appreciate everyone's
extra hours on this launch.
Crimson tag: Lie.
He only cares about his quarterly bonus.
A colleague leans over and whispers,
don't worry, your presentation was fantastic.
Crimson tag: Lie.
She did not listen to a single word.
Psychologist Robert Feldman discovered that
in an ordinary ten-minute conversation,
the average human tells two to three lies.
We do not do it because we are monsters.
We do it because radical honesty
is psychological warfare.
Imagine if everyone said,
I am bored of talking to you.
Your new haircut looks terrible.
I only invited you because I felt obligated.
Civilization survives on tiny white lies
like an engine survives on motor oil.
Without that oil,
human conversation grinds together
until the gears shatter.
By the end of your second day,
you are terrified to speak.
Because every time someone is nice to you,
the glowing red badge tells you:
They are only trying to survive the interaction.
By day four,
the small white lies stop bothering you.
It is the deeper lies that begin to tear you apart.
You meet your closest friend for coffee.
You ask him how he has been doing since his breakup.
He smiles and says,
honestly, I am completely over it.
I feel freer than ever.
Above his chest,
a soft red glow pulses:
Lie.
He cries himself to sleep every night.
Here, the crimson tag is not malice.
It is shame.
Humans lie to hide their bleeding wounds.
We lie so our friends will not
see how fragile we really are.
Then comes the real shock.
You ask him,
are we good?
You felt distant lately.
He pauses, looks at the table,
and says: I was envious of your promotion.
And I hated myself for feeling that way.
Above his words,
there is no red tag.
A soft emerald light illuminates the air:
Truth.
One hundred percent.
It hits you like a physical shock.
Hearing an ugly truth feels ten times more
loving than hearing a beautiful lie.
Because for the first time in your life,
you are meeting a human being without armor.
On the evening of day six,
you walk back to your apartment in complete silence.
You realize that you have spent
five days judging the world.
You analyzed your boss.
You tested your friends.
You graded every stranger on the subway.
So you walk into your bathroom.
You lock the door.
And you look straight into your own reflection.
I am happy with where I am in life,
you whisper.
Crimson flash: Lie.
I do not care what people think of me.
Crimson flash: Lie.
I have forgiven everyone who hurt me.
A violent red pulse:
Lie.
The tears start running down your cheeks.
The most dangerous deceiver in your life
was never your coworker or your partner.
It was you.
We tell ourselves comfortable fairy tales so
we do not have to face our fear of failure,
our grief, and our loneliness.
You stare into the mirror and finally say the
one thing you have avoided for ten years:
I am terrified of being alone.
And I am trying my best.
For the first time all week,
the crimson vanishes.
A deep, tranquil green envelops the glass:
Truth.
Absolute.
Midnight arrives on the seventh day.
The glowing tags fade into the quiet night air.
Over the last six weeks,
you have experienced every impossible power:
You saw the salaries of every neighbor
and realized wealth buys comfort,
not peace.
You saw the karma scores and learned
that morality is an inward discipline,
not a public spectacle.
You heard what people whispered behind your back
and found the freedom of not needing applause.
You tasted infinite save points and
discovered that life's beauty exists
only because mistakes are permanent.
You saw the countdown clocks of mortality
and learned that our limited time is
what makes every moment sacred.
And now, seeing every lie has
taught you the ultimate lesson:
Truth without empathy is cruelty.
And honesty without vulnerability
is just another weapon.
You step outside onto the morning sidewalk.
The barista hands you your cup and says,
have a wonderful day.
There is no green tag.
There is no red tag.
Just two strangers on a spinning rock,
trying to be kind to each other.
You smile back at her,
take a sip of hot coffee,
and whisper: Thank you.
And this time,
in your heart,
you know it is the absolute truth.
